content: Ascaris lumbricoides is a prevalent parasitic infection, particularly affecting children in low-income regions. Improving water and sanitation, providing health education, and administering effective drug treatments are key strategies to interrupt the transmission cycle and reduce associated morbidity. This study aimed to evaluate and compare the efficacy and safety of three anthelmintic drugs—albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin—for treating individuals with confirmed Ascaris infections. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Disease Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and LILACS, up to July 4, 2019. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared these drugs in both children and adults. Two reviewers independently assessed the studies for inclusion, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data, with a third reviewer verifying the data quality. The Cochrane 'Risk of bias' tool was used to assess study quality, and the GRADE approach was applied to determine the certainty of the evidence. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to compare treatment outcomes, and statistical models were chosen based on the level of heterogeneity. The analysis included 30 parallel-group RCTs involving 6,442 participants from 17 countries across Africa, Asia, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America. Participants ranged in age from 28 days to 82 years and were recruited from schools, communities, and healthcare facilities. Of these studies, 20 were funded or co-funded by drug manufacturers, while 10 were independently funded. Twenty-two trials exhibited a high risk of bias in one or two domains, such as blinding, incomplete outcome data, or selective reporting. A single dose of albendazole, mebendazole, or ivermectin was compared to placebo in several trials. Parasitological cure rates at 14 to 60 days post-treatment were significantly higher in the anthelmintic groups compared to placebo, with an illustrative cure rate of 93.0% in the treatment group versus 16.1% in the placebo group (RR 6.29, 95% CI 3.91 to 10.12; moderate-certainty evidence). A single dose of albendazole was found to be as effective as multiple doses of albendazole (93.2% vs. 94.3% cure rates; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.05; high-certainty evidence) and as effective as a single dose of mebendazole (98.0% vs. 96.9% cure rates; RR 1.01, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.02; high-certainty evidence). No significant difference was observed between a single dose of albendazole and a single dose of ivermectin (87.8% vs. 90.2% cure rates; RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.08; moderate-certainty evidence). Failure rates after a single dose of albendazole ranged from 0.0% to 30.3%, mebendazole from 0.0% to 22.2%, and ivermectin from 0.0% to 21.6%. The egg reduction rate (ERR) up to 60 days post-treatment was consistently high across all treatment groups, ranging from 96% to 100%, regardless of the drug used. However, the studies did not allow for an evaluation of parasitological cure rates based on the intensity of infection. None of the included trials reported complications or serious adverse events. Other adverse events were similar across the anthelmintic groups and were generally mild, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and fever (moderateto low-certainty evidence). In conclusion, single doses of albendazole, mebendazole, and ivermectin are all highly effective against Ascaris lumbricoides infection, achieving high parasitological cure rates and significant reductions in egg excretion. No significant differences in efficacy or adverse events were detected between the drugs. These medications appear to be safe for treating both children and adults with confirmed Ascaris infections, and there is little to distinguish between the drugs or dosing regimens in terms of outcomes.
